newsitem.title: GERMANY: FEATURE - East nostalgia strong six years after German unity.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE - East nostalgia strong six years after German unity.

text.p: He looks like Erich Honecker. Dresses, walks, and talks like Erich Honecker. And he even waves to the crowds like him.

Kurt Schmidt, a retired baker who bears a striking resemblance to the late ruler of communist East Germany, has become the favourite guest at scores of parties harking back to the country's Stalinist past.

Whether swinging his hips to techno versions of political songs or being escorted by long-legged girls in the uniforms of the defunct Communist youth organisation (FDJ), Schmidt -- so unlike the real Honecker -- is the ever-smiling centre of attention.

"People come up to me and shout "Erich is alive! Erich is alive!'" said Schmidt, 75, wearing black-rimmed glasses and snug-fitting tan suits identical to Honecker's. "I try to tell them, no Erich is dead. I'm Kurt. But they won't believe it.
"They tell me "Nooo! You can say whatever you want. Erich is alive. I saw him here!' They just won't believe it."

Six years after Germany unified on October 3, 1990, nostalgia for a lost eastern identity remains as powerful as it is improbable. The communist East German state's tight travel restrictions, its near-worthless currency and reviled Stasi security police are just distant memories now.
In its place there is a yearning for what now seem much happier days -- before the Berlin Wall fell and unemployment came, before housing costs surged and job security disappeared.
That longing is most visible at the "Ostalgie" (Eastern nostalgia) parties that attract up to 4,000 easterners ranging from their early teens to their late 80s into provincial discotheques.

They trundle by the thousands with their smoky little Trabant cars to vast discos in small eastern cities like Prenzlau to relive for a few glorious hours the cosier comforts of communist life and forget the colder capitalist Germany.

"I only need to start singing the first line of the old East German songs and the whole place immediately joins in," said Ralf Heckel, a disc jockey who has organised more than 40 "Ostalgie" parties attended by more than 60,000 easterners.

"Every Ossie (easterner) still knows these songs by heart," said Heckel, a 27-year-old entrepreneur whose tour group includes the Honecker double, a teenage singing group called the "Easty Girls", and erotic dancers called "The Magdeburger Models" who strip off their East German army uniforms.

"The atmosphere is just unbelievable," Heckel said. "It feels like in the old days. It's like a time machine. Everyone wants to relive that old feeling of camaraderie we had before. Even 80-year-old grannies call me up and ask if they can come."
While a good number of the older eastern Germans may miss the safety net of socialism and want East Germany back, most younger easterners at the parties are just looking for laughs.

Prenzlau, a decaying town 130 km (80 miles) north of Berlin, has a dwindling population of 27,000. With unemployment in the agricultural region well above 20 percent, many have packed up and left for jobs in western Germany.
Yet even in a place as small as Prenzlau, more than 1,500 crowded into a disco in a dilapidated empty factory district for the "Ostalgie" party.

They stood in long queues to buy their "visas" (entrance fee) and "exchange" their Deutsche marks for the Ostmarks needed inside to pay for drinks with such memorable names as "Lenin Vodka" and "Erich's Revenge."

Bouncers dressed in the uniforms of East German border guards checked the party-goers' ID cards, barmen clad in olive green uniforms of East German army officers talked about the good old days and everyone who wore "Free German Youth" (FDJ) shirts got in free.

"There were a lot of positive things about East Germany that people didn't appreciate then as much as they do now," said Heiko Kirschbaum, the co-owner of the Prenzlau disco that hosted one "Ostalgie" party.

"Everyone now has the material things they always dreamed of having, like a car or a video recorder, but they often don't have a job anymore," he added. "So many have lost their jobs, their places in society and their self-respect. It's no wonder they are happy to see Erich Honecker in here again."
The Honecker double, played with aplomb by Schmidt, is without doubt the highlight of the party. Schmidt is nine years younger than Honecker, who died in exile in Chile in 1994.
"Buenas Dias," Schmidt says in German-accented Spanish, greeting wide-eyed visitors who ponder: Could it really be him?

"I've looked like Erich for the last 30 years," said Schmidt. "Before it was something of a burden. But now I am filling a market niche," he added, smiling at his use of free market terminology that is still new to the east.

Although many western Germans are appalled by the "Ostalgie" and find it inconcievable that those who once risked their lives to escape the communist east would now flock to such celebrations, the fate of people like Hans-Dieter Uhlmann helps to shed light on the phenomenon.
Now an unhappy and under-employed construction worker, Uhlmann was a devoted "Volkspolizist" (People's Police officer) in Chemnitz who by all accounts loved his job.
But then came German unification. He was told to turn in his badge because he wore eyeglasses.

"Being a police officer was a deeply fulfilling profession for me," said 33-year-old Uhlmann. "It was the only career I ever wanted. But then they told me that they had enough other candidates with better eyesight. That hurt. It still hurts."
Last year Uhlmann heard about an "Ostalgie" party. He wore his old police uniform and had such a great time that he begged Heckel to join the travelling "Ostalgie" team.
Now, for a few magical hours every Saturday night, Hans-Dieter Uhlmann is a Volkspolizist again.
"It feels good," Uhlmann said. "It feels very good."
